Looking at this problem, I need to analyze the derived series of a finite solvable group.

## Analysis

**Setup.** Let $G$ be a non-trivial finite solvable group. Its derived series is
$$G = G^{(0)} \geq G^{(1)} \geq G^{(2)} \geq \cdots \geq G^{(n)} = \{e\},$$
where $G^{(i+1)} = [G^{(i)}, G^{(i)}]$. Since $G$ is solvable, the series terminates at the identity. The "smallest non-trivial group in the derived series" is the last non-trivial term $G^{(n-1)} \neq \{e\}$.

**Key fact 1: $G^{(n-1)}$ is abelian.** By definition, $G^{(n)} = [G^{(n-1)}, G^{(n-1)}] = \{e\}$, which means every pair of elements in $G^{(n-1)}$ commutes. So $G^{(n-1)}$ is an abelian group.

**Key fact 2: $G^{(n-1)}$ is normal in $G$.** Every term of the derived series is a characteristic subgroup of $G$ (each $G^{(i)}$ is fully invariant, hence characteristic, hence normal). In particular, $G^{(n-1)} \trianglelefteq G$.

**Key fact 3: Conjugacy classes of elements in $G^{(n-1)}$ stay inside $G^{(n-1)}$.** Since $G^{(n-1)} \trianglelefteq G$, for any $g \in G^{(n-1)}$ and any $h \in G$, we have $hgh^{-1} \in G^{(n-1)}$. Therefore the full conjugacy class
$$\mathrm{Cl}(g) = \{hgh^{-1} : h \in G\} \subseteq G^{(n-1)}.$$

**Conclusion.** Take any non-trivial element $g \in G^{(n-1)}$ (which exists since $G^{(n-1)} \neq \{e\}$). The subgroup generated by its conjugacy class satisfies:
$$\langle \mathrm{Cl}(g) \rangle \leq G^{(n-1)}.$$
Since $G^{(n-1)}$ is abelian, every subgroup of it is abelian. Therefore $\langle \mathrm{Cl}(g) \rangle$ is commutative.

Thus $G^{(n-1)}$ contains a non-trivial element (in fact, every non-trivial element) whose conjugacy class generates a commutative subgroup.

## Answer

**Yes.** In a finite solvable group, the smallest non-trivial term $G^{(n-1)}$ of the derived series is always abelian and normal in $G$. For any non-trivial $g \in G^{(n-1)}$, normality forces $\mathrm{Cl}(g) \subseteq G^{(n-1)}$, so $\langle \mathrm{Cl}(g) \rangle \leq G^{(n-1)}$ is abelian. Hence such an element always exists.
